quote: “Scarcity,” it’s called in social psychology. What appears to be in limited supply is more highly valued. And this effect is especially strong with information—we’re much more likely to try to obtain information that we believe is secret, and to value it more when we do obtain it.
content: The literature supports the first sentence, weakly, and does not contain the second. Commodity theory’s meta-analysis (Lynn (1991)) finds that unavailability raises rated value by a moderate amount, mostly for items already assumed desirable; the information-specific evidence is a handful of studies (Brock’s own, and the banned-speech study in Scarcity) measuring momentary attitude change, not effort. No study shows that making information secret increases the sustained work of acquiring it, which is what “study science” requires, and the closest natural experiments cut the other way: the fields that guarded their knowledge (alchemy, the craft guilds, the Pythagoreans of the legend) trained few and progressed slowly, and the open-science norms of the seventeenth century, priority by publication and disclosure of method, are the standard explanation for why the rate of discovery changed (David (2008)). The essay extrapolates from a valuation effect measured in minutes to a motivational effect that would have to last years, and the historical record of secret knowledge is the record of that extrapolation failing.

quote: When you look at it from that perspective, the escape of math from the Pythagorean cult starts to look like a major strategic blunder for humanity.
content: The Pythagorean secrecy the essay has in mind is mostly legend. The story that Hippasus was drowned for revealing the irrationality of √2 is told by Iamblichus about eight centuries after the fact, in different versions attributing it to different disclosures, and Burkert’s reconstruction (Lore and Science in Ancient Pythagoreanism, 1972) finds the early Pythagoreans to have been a religious brotherhood whose “mathematics” was numerology; the mathematical tradition that produced Euclid ran through the open schools of Athens and Alexandria and owed the Pythagoreans little beyond a name. Greek mathematics did not escape from a cult; it grew up outside one. And the experiment the essay muses about was run at scale: alchemy kept its Great Truths secret from the Hellenistic period to the eighteenth century, produced a vast literature of initiation, allegory and guarded recipe, and yielded chemistry only when Boyle and his successors began publishing what they did. Newton, who spent years on the secret tradition, published his optics and mechanics and kept his alchemy in manuscript; the half he published is the half that mattered.

quote: Right now, we’ve got the worst of both worlds. Science isn’t really free, because the courses are expensive and the textbooks are expensive. But the public thinks that anyone is allowed to know, so it must not be important.
content: The decade after this essay made science nearly free in fact: massive open online courses, Khan Academy, open textbooks, arXiv for physics, Sci-Hub for the paywalled journals. The result tests the essay’s hypothesis from both sides. Availability alone did not produce mass study; MOOC completion rates settled around five to ten per cent and were falling (Reich & Ruipérez-Valiente (2019)), which is consistent with the essay’s view that free access is not the binding constraint. But the courses that did retain learners did so with credentials, cohorts, deadlines and status, not with secrecy; the mechanism that works is the one the essay describes as science’s existing “initiation rituals both social and cognitive,” scaled up and made cheap. Nothing in the record suggests that a vault would have done better than a certificate. The essay’s diagnosis, that people take their cues about importance from others’ attitudes, is right; its prescription confuses the cue that matters, whether other people one respects are doing it, with a cue that might be faked, whether one is forbidden.
